channel.title: Almost Lore
channel.description: Original longform on documented historical near-misses and the odder corners of the public record.

item.title: The war named for a pig
item.description: In June 1859 an American settler shot a Hudson’s Bay Company boar on an island the Oregon Treaty had failed to assign. Troops landed. The commemorative line says the pig was the only casualty. The record is a thirteen-year occupation and a boundary drawn in 1872.

item.title: The Caroline at Schlosser
item.description: On the night of 29 December 1837 a British party burned the American steamer Caroline at a landing on the New York side of the Niagara. Amos Durfee was killed on the dock. The near-war was not a second battle at the river. It was a murder charge, a boast, and a sentence about necessity that the two governments adopted without agreeing the raid had earned it.

item.title: Searchlights on the Dogger Bank
item.description: On the night of 21–22 October 1904 a Russian squadron on its way to the war with Japan fired on Hull trawlers over the Dogger Bank. A commission of inquiry counted two fishermen dead and one trawler sunk, and a majority found no torpedo boats there to fire at. Britain and Russia stayed at peace. The report’s own courtesies are why the outrage and the file are not the same story.

item.title: The four men taken off the Trent
item.description: On 8 November 1861 a Union captain stopped the British mail steamer Trent in the Old Bahama Channel and took off two Confederate commissioners and their secretaries. No one was killed. The near-war was the month Britain spent demanding them back, and the note that gave them back without settling the law.

item.title: Every means in its power
item.description: In December 1895 Grover Cleveland told Congress the United States would resist, by every means in its power, a British hold on any land an American commission decided belonged to Venezuela. Britain had just refused to arbitrate the whole boundary. No troops met. The near-miss ended in a treaty, a fifty-year prescription rule, and a line Venezuela later refused to treat as the last word.

item.title: A line convenient to both
item.description: In February 1839 the lieutenant-governor of New Brunswick told Maine to pull an armed posse off the Aroostook or he would occupy the disputed territory. On 3 March Congress appropriated ten million dollars and, if invasion was imminent, a ceiling of fifty thousand volunteers. The papers of that winter contain an arrest, a parole, and a threat. They do not contain a battle. The line signed in August 1842 was a conventional boundary, not a finding that the highlands of 1783 had been located.

item.title: The fog that was not weather
item.description: In late September 1950 a Navy vessel sprayed bacteria over San Francisco from offshore. The city was not told. The Army later said the organisms were harmless. Stanford Hospital then recorded a rare Serratia cluster, and one man died.

item.title: The island that kept the captain
item.description: In November 1741 Vitus Bering’s ship wrecked on an uninhabited island off Kamchatka. He died there on 8 December. Forty-six of the crew got a smaller boat home the next summer, and with them the news that the American coast was not a rumor.

item.title: The isthmus that was supposed to pay Scotland
item.description: In July 1698 five Scottish ships carried about twelve hundred people to Darien and called the place Caledonia. They abandoned it in 1699. A second fleet, already at sea, found the fort empty, refounded it, and surrendered to Spain in the spring of 1700.

item.title: Two flags at Fashoda
item.description: In 1898 a French column and an Anglo-Egyptian flotilla met at a ruined fort on the White Nile. Neither side fired. Europe spent the autumn deciding whether that counted as a war.

item.title: The country that existed on paper
item.description: Gregor MacGregor did not invent a rumor. He invented offices, banknotes, a loan, and a sailing date — then sent people to a shore that had none of the city he sold.

item.title: Aqua Tofana, after the legend
item.description: The poison that killed six hundred husbands is a later story. The Roman archive holds a 1659 prosecution, a sealed transcript, and a woman popularly called Tofana who was already dead.

item.title: One hundred and ten miles of Atlantic
item.description: In July 1978 Don Cameron and Christopher Davey flew Zanussi from Newfoundland toward Europe, leaked, tore, and ditched in the Bay of Biscay. The first successful crossing landed three weeks later.

item.title: The subway that ran one block
item.description: Alfred Ely Beach’s 1870 pneumatic tube under Broadway was a working passenger demo, a political long shot, and a civic almost. New York’s real subway opened thirty-four years later.
